title: Someone force-pushed over main and deleted a day of commits
summary: Six commits vanished from the shared main. Find them in a colleague's clone, restore the branch on the server, and install the protection that makes it impossible next time.
mental_model: A force push replaces the server's ref. The commits are not deleted from the server's object database immediately, and every clone that fetched them still has them — so recovery is about finding any copy and pushing it back.

setup.run: git commit -q -m "Local experiment that should never have been pushed"

steps.title: Assess the damage on the server
steps.why: The bare repository is the source of truth for the team, and four commits of work are simply not in it any more. Establish the scope before touching anything.
steps.expect: Two commits, and no payments, refunds or audit files.

steps.title: Find a clone that still has them
steps.why: Anyone who fetched before the force push still holds the commits and, crucially, a remote-tracking reflog recording where origin/main used to point. That reflog is the recovery key.
steps.expect: After fetching, origin/main moves back — but the reflog still records the old sha.

verify.label: the colleague's remote-tracking reflog has the pre-force position

steps.title: Confirm the old commits are intact in that clone
steps.why: `origin/main@{1}` names where the ref pointed one move ago. Everything is there — the force push removed a pointer, not the objects in this clone.
steps.expect: Six commits, and the payment code readable.

verify.label: the lost work is fully present in the colleague's clone

steps.title: Rescue them onto a branch first
steps.why: Name them before doing anything else. A branch makes the commits reachable and safe from garbage collection while you decide how to restore them.

verify.label: the lost history has a name again

steps.title: Decide what main should be
steps.why: The rescued history plus the one commit that was force-pushed on top. Rather than discarding anyone's work, rebase the stray commit onto the restored line — the honest outcome for a shared branch.
steps.expect: Two histories: five rescued commits, and two containing the stray experiment.

steps.title: Rebuild main and push it back
steps.why: Replay the stray commit onto the rescued tip, then force-push once, deliberately, having looked at exactly what you are replacing. This is the only force push in the incident that anyone should make.

verify.label: the server has the restored history plus the stray commit
verify.hint: cherry-pick the stray commit onto the rescued tip, then push --force once

steps.title: Install the protection
steps.why: The incident was possible because the server accepted a non-fast-forward push to main. A pre-receive hook — or branch protection on a forge — turns this from an incident into an error message.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Refuse non-fast-forward pushes and deletions on main.
ZERO=0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
status=0

while read old new ref; do
  [ "$ref" = "refs/heads/main" ] || continue
  if [ "$new" = "$ZERO" ]; then
    echo "pre-receive: refusing to delete main" >&2
    status=1
  elif [ "$old" != "$ZERO" ] && ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$old" "$new"; then
    echo "pre-receive: refusing force push to main" >&2
    status=1
  fi
done
exit $status

steps.expect: The next force push is rejected — the hole is closed.

verify.label: the protection held: main was not rewound again
verify.hint: a pre-receive hook comparing old and new with merge-base --is-ancestor

verify.label: the server's main has the recovered history
verify.hint: rescue from a colleague's origin/main@{1}, then push it back

verify.label: the lost payment code is back on the server

pitfalls: Act before the reflogs expire and before anyone runs `gc --prune=now` on the server. Recovery windows are days, not months.
`origin/main@{1}` exists only in clones that had fetched the good state. Ask the whole team before concluding the commits are gone.
Do not let people 'fix' it by re-pushing their own stale main — that compounds the damage with a second force push.
The server's own reflog (`core.logAllRefUpdates` on a bare repo) can also hold the old tip, but it is off by default for bare repositories.
The permanent fix is server-side. Asking people to be careful with `--force` has never worked anywhere.
